title: RECON: Robust symmetry discovery via Explicit Canonical Orientation Normalization
one_liner: A method that corrects how models ground their coordinate systems to discover and align to real-world symmetries without retraining.
lead: Real-world objects have hidden symmetries — a face looks the same rotated 30 degrees either way, a molecule has mirror-plane symmetries. When a model learns to recognize these objects, it should line them up to a single reference direction so it treats all equivalent rotations the same. Most models pick a reference direction arbitrarily, leaving different examples pointing in wildly different compass directions even when they are the same physical object. RECON discovers the real shared symmetry pattern hidden in the data and realigns all examples to it, so downstream classifiers see each symmetry-equivalent form in the same pose.

problem.h2: Arbitrary reference frames break symmetry learning
paras: When you teach a model to recognize objects, you often tell it: 'first extract what the object is (invariant features), then track which direction it is pointing (pose).' The problem: every class gets assigned a reference direction by whoever is training the model — it could be 'nose points up' or 'nose points left', chosen once and frozen. If you train on faces with noses pointing up, and later see faces with noses pointing left, the model treats them as completely different patterns, even though they are the same face.

A naive approach tries: 'I will pick one canonical (reference) direction per class and measure pose relative to that.' But this fails because the canonical direction is arbitrary. Two models trained identically will pick different canonicals, and real data does not naturally align to arbitrary choices. The model sees pose as drifting wildly across the data, making it impossible to learn a clean, shared symmetry pattern.

callout.html: Models ground pose (rotation/orientation) to arbitrary training-chosen reference frames, not to real symmetries in the data. This hides the true symmetry pattern in the data.

steps.b: Step 1: Collect examples nearby in invariant space
steps.text: For input x, find k nearest neighbors in the model's learned feature space (the invariant embedding). These neighbors are perceptually similar — same class, different rotations.
Extract the pose (a rotation or group element) that the model predicted for each neighbor. These poses are currently scattered in arbitrary directions relative to the model's chosen canonical frame.
Find the central direction in which all these poses point. This is the true shared symmetry distribution. Compute the correction: a single transformation that aligns all poses to this center.
Right-multiply each pose by the inverse of the centering transformation. This rotates every pose into alignment without touching the class features.

steps.b: Step 5: Use corrected poses at test time
steps.text: Feed the original image through the correction layer, canonicalizing it to the natural reference frame. Downstream classifier now sees examples in aligned poses, improving accuracy.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the reference frame
paras: The paper does not redesign the model or the learning process. Instead, it adds one line: a test-time canonicalization layer that corrects the reference frame to match reality. It replaces the model's arbitrary, training-picked canonical with one that aligns to the real symmetry pattern in the data.

hidden.name: natural pose distribution
paras: Every object has a true distribution of rotations in which it appears in real data. A face might appear in a natural range from −30° to +30°; a molecule might have mirror symmetries baked in. This is the hidden quantity: the real pose distribution that raw, unlabeled data exhibits. It is hidden because the model's arbitrary canonical frame has tilted and scrambled it so it looks scattered and per-class different.

The paper estimates it by looking at which poses cluster together when you find neighbors that are perceptually identical (same invariant features). If ten neighbors all tend to point in roughly the same direction when you look at their raw poses, that direction is the natural center. RECON computes this center for every equivalence class (similar-looking examples) and uses it to correct the pose output.

heat.caption: Highlighted: examples with aligned natural poses (w2, w3, w5, w9, w11). Dim: outliers and errors.

reads.html: The true pose distribution is the pattern of rotations (or orientations) you actually see in real, unlabeled examples. It is what data naturally exhibits, not what the training pipeline invented.

In the paper's notation, the natural pose distribution is the set of group elements that maintain the invariant component (the class features). RECON infers it by collecting the poses of k-nearest neighbors in feature space and centering them via a transformation derived from neighborhood consensus.

mechanism.h2: How correcting the reference frame fixes the problem
paras: Here is the causal chain: Models learn to decompose inputs into class (what) and pose (direction). But they ground pose to an arbitrary reference — whatever the training loop happened to pick first. So two examples that are truly the same rotation end up with different pose numbers, because they are being measured relative to different training-chosen canonicals.

RECON detects which examples are truly the same (by finding them as nearest neighbors in feature space) and looks at their raw poses. It notices: they all point roughly the same direction in the model's output space, even though the model thinks they are different. That consistency is the signal. RECON computes a single correction matrix (the centering transformation) that brings all those poses into alignment. When you right-multiply each pose by this correction, you rotate them from the arbitrary training-frame into the natural data-aligned frame.

Why does this help the downstream classifier? Because now when it sees a new face at −10°, the invariant features stay the same, but the pose vectors all point to the same region (the natural distribution). The classifier learns a single decision boundary for 'face in natural pose range' instead of learning separate boundaries for 'face in Class-A-canonical-frame' and 'face in Class-B-canonical-frame'. No retraining needed — the correction happens once, at test time, on top of the frozen model.

stages.s: Compute invariant embedding (what-is-it) via frozen encoder
Retrieve k nearest neighbors in feature space
Gather their pose vectors, find center (Γ−1)
Right-multiply input pose by correction matrix
Canonicalized image in natural pose frame; feed to frozen classifier

math.words: For each input, compute the centered pose by right-multiplying the model's output pose by a correction transformation. The correction is the inverse of the average direction detected in a neighborhood. Mathematically: adjusted_pose = original_pose times (centering_transformation)^−1.
symbols: the corrected pose distribution after centering
the original pose vectors for examples in the neighborhood
the centering transformation (the average direction in the neighborhood)
the inverse correction (rotates back to align everything)
the equivalence class (neighbors similar to x in invariant space)

worked.title: Tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the invariant encoder says three neighbors belong together: [x1, x2, x3].
Their original poses (angles) are: ψ(x1) = 10°, ψ(x2) = 15°, ψ(x3) = 12°.
Average direction: Γ = 12.3°. Correction: Γ^-1 = −12.3° (inverse rotation).
All three now centered near 0°. The downstream classifier sees them in the same reference frame.

math.note: The right-multiplication corrects the pose without changing the invariant features, aligning all examples to the natural symmetry distribution discovered in the data.

bars.h2: Comparing arbitrary canonicals to data-aligned canonicals

charts.title: Arbitrary canonical (baseline)
charts.note: The model's chosen reference frame is orthogonal to reality. Different rotations scatter into different distributions, confusing the classifier.

charts.title: RECON (data-aligned canonical)
charts.note: Natural canonicalization aligns poses to the true pattern, so the downstream classifier sees all equivalent rotations looking identical. That sameness means the classifier learns a single decision boundary instead of splitting the boundary across many angle offsets, so it works better on new data.

items.html: If the invariant feature space is noisy or the model has not learned good class-disentangled representations, k-nearest neighbors will grab wrong neighbors. Then the centering transformation aligns to noise instead of real symmetry. Result: pose correction fails.

Some objects might naturally have multiple disconnected pose families (e.g., left-facing and right-facing forms, not a smooth continuum). A single global centering transformation cannot handle this; it will average conflicting symmetries. The method assumes unimodal or near-unimodal pose distributions.

If test examples exhibit poses far outside the training distribution (a face at 90° when training only saw −30° to +30°), the centering transformation was learned on training neighborhoods and cannot correct out-of-distribution poses. Detection is possible (part of the method), but correction fails.

The method succeeds when the invariant encoder is accurate, training data covers the natural pose range well, and the pose family is unimodal (one connected symmetry distribution). In these cases, RECON gives free accuracy gains on any frozen pre-trained classifier.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Write a small notebook that: (1) loads a pre-trained class-pose decomposition model (e.g., an IE-AE variant) on a rotation-equivariance dataset (FashionMNIST with known rotations, or 3D objects), (2) applies RECON's centering algorithm to the test set by finding k-nearest neighbors in invariant space and computing pose corrections, (3) passes both uncorrected and corrected test images through a frozen downstream classifier (e.g., a simple linear model trained on original canonical poses), (4) measures accuracy, pose alignment quality (hit-rate metric), and out-of-distribution pose detection performance.
demo.closing: The demo must show: (1) corrected poses clustering tightly in the natural distribution while uncorrected poses spread wide, (2) downstream accuracy rising without any retraining, (3) out-of-distribution poses correctly flagged as unreliable.
